title: 5 Best AI Prompts for System Design Interviews (2026)
description: Practice system design with an AI interviewer that pushes back: requirements, architecture, deep-dives, failure drills, and a brutal mock with grading.

steps.title: Requirements interrogation
steps.promptText:
You are a FAANG staff engineer conducting a system design interview. The problem: design [SYSTEM — e.g. "a URL shortener" / "Instagram stories"].

Start by making ME do the requirements: ask one clarifying question at a time (functional, scale, latency, consistency), push back when my answers are vague, and after 6-8 exchanges, summarize the requirements WE agreed and state the 2-3 numbers that will drive the whole design (QPS, storage, read/write ratio).
steps.whyThisTool: One-question-at-a-time forces the interview rhythm real interviews have — no info dumps.
steps.outputExpected: An agreed requirements sheet with the load numbers that anchor every later decision.

steps.title: Architecture with trade-offs spoken aloud
steps.promptText:
Now I'll propose my high-level architecture: [DESCRIBE YOUR DESIGN OR SAY "walk me through building it Socratically"].

Respond as the interviewer: for each component I name, ask WHY over the obvious alternative (SQL vs NoSQL, push vs pull, cache where?). Don't accept "for scalability" — demand the specific property that matters here. Keep score of trade-offs I articulate well vs. hand-wave.
steps.whyThisTool: The 'don't accept scalability as an answer' rule trains the articulation interviews actually grade.
steps.outputExpected: A dialogue where every design choice got defended — and a running list of your hand-waves.

steps.title: Deep-dive drill
steps.promptText: Pick the component in my design most likely to be probed in a real interview and drill it: data model, exact read/write paths, what's in memory vs disk, the specific numbers (can one node hold it? partition how?). When I answer, follow up twice more before moving on — interviews go 3 levels deep, so practice should.
steps.whyThisTool: Three-levels-deep questioning exposes whether you know it or just know its name.
steps.outputExpected: A component you can now discuss to the level of bytes and partitions.

steps.title: Failure and scale drills
steps.promptText: Run failure drills on my design, one at a time: the cache cluster dies, traffic 10x's during a launch, one region loses network, a celebrity user creates a hot key. For each: ask what breaks first, wait for my answer, then correct or extend it. End with the 3 changes that most improve resilience per unit of complexity.
steps.whyThisTool: Failure drills are the highest-signal part of senior interviews and the least practiced.
steps.outputExpected: A prioritized resilience shortlist and confidence discussing cascading failures.

steps.title: Full mock with grading
steps.promptText: Full mock: 35 minutes, [NEW SYSTEM]. You run it exactly like rounds 1-4 combined, timed pacing included ("we have 10 minutes left, let's discuss..."). Afterward grade me on the real rubric: requirements, high-level design, deep dive, trade-offs, communication — each 1-5 with the specific moment that earned the score, plus the ONE thing to fix before my real interview.
steps.whyThisTool: A graded mock with cited moments beats generic 'good job' feedback by a mile.
steps.outputExpected: A rubric scorecard and one concrete, highest-leverage improvement.

faq.q: Is practicing with AI as good as mock interviews with humans?
faq.a: It's 80% as good and 100x more available. Use AI for reps and drills, then spend your scarce human mocks validating under real social pressure.

faq.q: Which system should I start with?
faq.a: URL shortener or rate limiter first (they exercise the fundamentals), then one read-heavy feed system, then one write-heavy system like chat. This pack works for all of them.

faq.q: ChatGPT or Claude for interview practice?
faq.a: Both hold the interviewer role well. Claude sustains the one-question-at-a-time discipline over long sessions slightly better, which is why we verify against it.

benefit: Walk into your system design interview having already survived five hard ones.
